title: HTTP Caching: The Field Handbook
summary: A practical deep-dive into how HTTP caching actually works — freshness and Cache-Control directives, validators and conditional revalidation, Vary and content negotiation, immutable fingerprinted assets, and how CDNs and shared caches change the rules. Ends with the mistakes that bite in production and a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Why Caching Exists & Where Caches Live
points: Caching = storing a response so a later equivalent request is served without a full origin round-trip
Three wins: latency (no RTT), bandwidth (no bytes), origin load (no compute/DB hit)
Private cache = browser HTTP cache, per-user, per-profile, on disk/memory
Shared cache = CDN edge, reverse proxy (nginx/Varnish), corporate forward proxy — serves many users
Cache hierarchy on a real request: memory cache → browser disk cache → Service Worker Cache API → CDN edge → shard/origin shield → origin
Only safe methods are cacheable by default: GET (and HEAD); POST is cacheable only with explicit freshness and is rarely done
Cache key by default = method + full URL (scheme, host, path, query string); ?v=2 is a different resource entirely
Vary headers extend the cache key with named request headers (Chapter 6)
Cacheable-by-default status codes: 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, 501 — yes, errors cache
Heuristic caching: with no Cache-Control and no Expires, a cache MAY guess freshness, commonly 10% of (Date − Last-Modified)
Gotcha: 'no cache headers' does not mean 'not cached' — it means 'cached by heuristic you don't control'
Caching is a correctness/performance trade: every cached byte is a bet that the origin hasn't changed
Terms: fresh (usable without asking), stale (past lifetime, must revalidate or be allowed to serve stale)

chapters.title: Freshness: Cache-Control Lifetime Directives
points: Cache-Control is the modern control surface; response directives are comma-separated, order-insensitive
max-age=N — response is fresh for N seconds after it was generated (age-relative, not clock-relative)
s-maxage=N — overrides max-age for shared caches only; browser keeps max-age, CDN uses s-maxage
Classic split: `Cache-Control: max-age=0, s-maxage=600` — browser always asks, CDN absorbs the load for 10 min
Expires: <HTTP-date> is the HTTP/1.0 predecessor; Cache-Control: max-age wins whenever both are present
Pragma: no-cache is a request-side HTTP/1.0 relic; never send it on responses, it does nothing useful
Age header = seconds the response has been sitting in shared caches; remaining freshness = max-age − Age
Freshness lifetime is computed from Date, not from when your browser received it — a CDN hit can arrive already 500s old
public — explicitly cacheable by shared caches, even for requests with Authorization headers
private — only the browser may store it; CDNs must not. Use for per-user HTML and dashboards
no-store — never write to any cache, memory or disk. The only real 'do not keep this' directive
no-cache is a lie by name: it means store it, but revalidate every time before reuse
must-revalidate — once stale, a cache must not serve it without checking origin (kills stale-on-error fallbacks)
proxy-revalidate = must-revalidate, but only binding on shared caches
Rule of thumb: `no-store` for secrets, `no-cache` for HTML, `max-age=31536000, immutable` for hashed assets

chapters.title: Validators: ETag and Last-Modified
points: A validator is a token the client sends back so the origin can answer 'unchanged' cheaply
ETag: opaque server-chosen version tag, e.g. `ETag: "a4f2c9"` — quoted string, contents meaningless to the client
Strong ETag `"abc"` = byte-for-byte identical; required for Range requests and safe partial reassembly
Weak ETag `W/"abc"` = semantically equivalent, bytes may differ (whitespace, timestamp comment, different gzip level)
Last-Modified: <HTTP-date> — 1-second resolution, so sub-second edits are invisible to it
Last-Modified fails on: files touched by deploy/rsync, content generated per-request, clock skew across origin servers
ETag beats Last-Modified on precision; Last-Modified beats ETag on multi-server consistency if ETags are inode-derived
Send both when you can — clients echo both, and the origin can pick the cheaper comparison
Common generation strategies: content hash (best), version+path, mtime+size (nginx default), DB row updated_at + id
Anti-pattern: inode-based ETags across a load-balanced fleet — same file, different ETag per box, zero hit rate
nginx generates `ETag: "mtime-hex-size-hex"`; Apache's FileETag INode is the classic multi-server footgun
Compression changes bytes: gzip and brotli variants need distinct strong ETags or a weak ETag
Cost model: computing a content-hash ETag per request can cost more than just sending the body — hash at build/write time

chapters.title: Revalidation: The Conditional Request Dance
points: When a stored response goes stale, the cache revalidates instead of refetching blind
If-None-Match: "a4f2c9" — echoes the stored ETag; the primary conditional header
If-Modified-Since: <date> — echoes the stored Last-Modified; used only when no ETag exists
If both are sent, the origin MUST evaluate If-None-Match and ignore If-Modified-Since
304 Not Modified = empty body, and the cache refreshes stored headers from the 304 and restarts the clock
A 304 must carry updated Cache-Control/ETag/Date; forgetting this makes the entry re-stale immediately, revalidating on every hit
200 with a full body = the resource changed; the cache replaces the entry wholesale
Comparison: strong compare (byte-identical, needed for Range) vs weak compare (used by If-None-Match on GET)
If-Match / If-Unmodified-Since are the write-side twins: optimistic concurrency for PUT/PATCH/DELETE
412 Precondition Failed = someone else wrote first; this is how you avoid lost updates on a REST API
`If-Match: *` means 'must already exist'; `If-None-Match: *` on PUT means 'create only if absent'
Revalidation still costs a full RTT — it saves bytes, not latency; that's why immutable assets matter
Request-side Cache-Control: no-cache is what a browser hard-reload (Ctrl+Shift+R) sends; max-age=0 is a normal reload
Example round trip: GET /app.css → 200 + ETag → later GET with If-None-Match → 304, ~200 bytes on the wire

chapters.title: Stale Serving: SWR, stale-if-error, and Collapsing
points: stale-while-revalidate=N — serve the stale copy instantly, refresh in the background for up to N seconds past expiry
`Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300` — one user pays the miss, everyone else gets an instant hit
SWR removes revalidation latency from the critical path; the cost is a bounded window of stale content
stale-if-error=N — if the origin returns 5xx/times out, keep serving the stale copy for N seconds
stale-if-error turns an origin outage into slightly-old content instead of a 502 wall
must-revalidate disables both stale behaviours — never pair it with stale-if-error and expect a fallback
Request collapsing / coalescing: N concurrent misses for the same key become 1 origin request
Cache stampede (dogpile): a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the origin in the same instant
Stampede defences: collapsing, SWR, jittered TTLs, early recomputation before expiry, origin shield tier
Jitter example: max-age = 3600 + rand(0..600) so a mass-populated cache doesn't expire in lockstep
Negative caching: cache 404s and 5xx briefly (5–30s) so a broken path can't hammer the origin
Trade-off: negative caching a 500 during a deploy can pin the error in place — keep those TTLs tiny
Serving stale is a product decision, not just an engineering one: agree what staleness is acceptable per route

chapters.title: Vary and Content Negotiation
points: Vary lists request headers that are part of the cache key: `Vary: Accept-Encoding`
Without Vary: Accept-Encoding, a brotli body can be served to a client that only accepts gzip — corrupted page
Vary: Accept-Encoding is the near-universal correct default whenever you compress
Each distinct header value creates a separate stored variant — cardinality is multiplicative across listed headers
Vary: User-Agent is a hit-rate catastrophe: thousands of UA strings, effectively one variant per visitor
Vary: Cookie is nearly as bad — every session ID is its own variant; usually you wanted `private` instead
Vary: * means 'never reusable' — equivalent to opting out of shared caching entirely
Vary: Accept-Language is legitimate but should be normalized to a small set (en, fr, de) before it hits the key
Vary: Origin is required when you reflect an Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, or you leak CORS grants across sites
Normalize at the edge: collapse Accept-Encoding to gzip|br|none, then Vary on the normalized value
CDNs often let you define the cache key directly (device class, country, a single cookie) — safer than raw Vary
Content negotiation alternative: separate URLs per variant (/img/hero.avif vs /img/hero.jpg) — no Vary, perfect hit rate
Debug rule: if hit rate is mysteriously ~0%, print the response Vary header first

chapters.title: Immutable Assets & Cache Busting
points: The core pattern: content-hash the filename, then cache the file forever — app.9f2c1a.js
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` — one year (the practical max) plus a no-revalidate promise
immutable tells the browser: do not even revalidate on reload; without it, a plain refresh still fires If-None-Match on every asset
Content changes ⇒ the hash changes ⇒ the URL changes ⇒ a new cache entry. Old entries just age out harmlessly
Query-string busting (app.js?v=3) is weaker: some intermediary proxies refuse to cache URLs with query strings
Never fingerprint your HTML entry point — it's the mutable index that points at the immutable assets
Canonical two-tier policy: HTML `no-cache` (or max-age=0, must-revalidate), assets `max-age=31536000, immutable`
Atomicity rule: deploy new assets BEFORE flipping HTML, and keep old assets live for at least one TTL window
Skipping that ordering = a client on old HTML requests a deleted chunk → chunk-load-error white screen
Version your API responses with ETags instead of hashed URLs — endpoints are addressed by meaning, not by build
Purging vs busting: purge is an out-of-band CDN API call, fragile and eventually-consistent; busting is inherent and instant
Purge by surrogate key/tag (Fastly, Cloudflare Enterprise): tag responses at edge, invalidate a whole content group in one call
Service Worker adds a fourth cache you own in JS — it can serve a stale app forever if you never call skipWaiting/claim
Sanity check: `curl -I` the asset and confirm age climbs on repeat calls while the ETag stays fixed

chapters.title: CDN Behaviour and the Edge Layer
points: A CDN is a shared cache with PoPs near users; a hit avoids both the origin RTT and the origin work
Cache states in headers: HIT, MISS, EXPIRED (revalidated), STALE, BYPASS, DYNAMIC — read x-cache / cf-cache-status / x-served-by
Origin shield: one designated mid-tier PoP fronts the origin so 200 edges produce 1 miss, not 200
Tiered caching turns hit ratio math around: edge hit ratio and origin offload ratio are different numbers, track both
Surrogate-Control and CDN-Cache-Control are edge-only headers, stripped before the browser sees them
Precedence at a well-behaved CDN: CDN-Cache-Control > Surrogate-Control > s-maxage > max-age
This lets you say 'edge caches 1 day, browser caches 60s' without a single custom rule in the CDN UI
Most CDNs bypass cache by default when a Set-Cookie is present on the response — one stray cookie kills your hit rate
Many CDNs also bypass when the request carries Authorization, unless the response is explicitly `public`
Cache key control: strip tracking params (utm_*, fbclid, gclid) or they shard one page into a thousand entries
Normalize before keying: lowercase host, sort query params, drop trailing slash inconsistencies
ESI / edge fragments and CDN-side HTML caching let you cache the shell and hole-punch the personalized parts
Cache poisoning: an unkeyed input (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Original-URL) reflected into the response, stored, then served to everyone
Defence: never reflect unkeyed request headers into cached output; key on anything that changes the body
Measure it: hit ratio, origin offload %, p50/p99 by cache state, bytes served from edge

chapters.title: Trade-offs, Comparisons and Cost Models
points: Latency ladder: memory cache ~0ms, disk cache ~1ms, CDN edge ~10–30ms, cross-region origin ~150ms+
Cost of a 304: full RTT + ~200 bytes. Cost of a fresh hit: 0. That gap is the entire argument for immutable
Long TTL = high hit rate + slow invalidation. Short TTL = fast propagation + heavy origin load. Pick per route
Expiration (TTL) vs invalidation (purge): expiration is cheap and eventual; invalidation is precise and operationally expensive
ETag vs Last-Modified: precision and per-request cost vs cheapness and 1s granularity
no-store vs no-cache vs max-age=0: never store / store-but-always-ask / stale immediately, then normal stale rules apply
private vs no-store: private still writes to the user's disk — not good enough for tokens on a shared machine
max-age vs s-maxage: the standard way to give browsers a short leash and CDNs a long one
Hashed URLs vs purge API: build-time correctness vs runtime coordination; prefer hashing whenever the client can be told a new URL
SWR vs must-revalidate: availability and speed vs strict freshness — a correctness decision per resource
Hit ratio is not the goal: origin offload and p99 latency are. A 99% hit rate on tiny assets can hide a hot uncached HTML route
Cache size is finite — LRU eviction means a huge long-tail asset set can push out your hot files
Rough capacity math: 1M req/day at 90% hit = 100k origin req/day ≈ ~1.2 rps; at 50% it's 500k ≈ ~6 rps
Every caching layer you add is another place truth can diverge — count your layers before adding one more

chapters.title: Common Mistakes + Cheat Sheet
points: Caching authenticated HTML on a shared cache — user A sees user B's dashboard. Use `private, no-store` for personalized pages
Assuming no-cache means don't cache; it means always revalidate. `no-store` is the one you wanted
Setting max-age=31536000 on a non-fingerprinted URL — you just pinned bad content on real browsers for a year with no recall
Forgetting Vary: Accept-Encoding — clients receive a body in an encoding they can't decode
Vary: User-Agent or Vary: Cookie 'to be safe' — you've disabled shared caching and doubled origin load
Returning a 304 without refreshed Cache-Control/ETag — the entry stays stale and revalidates on every single request
Inode-derived ETags across a fleet — same content, different validator per server, near-zero revalidation savings
Set-Cookie on a static asset response — most CDNs will refuse to cache it, silently
Deleting old build artifacts on deploy — in-flight clients on the old HTML hit 404 chunks and white-screen
Purging as a routine workflow instead of an emergency tool — it doesn't scale and it's eventually consistent
Not caching 404s at all — a scanner or broken link becomes free origin load
Trusting a hard-reload to test caching: Ctrl+Shift+R sends `Cache-Control: no-cache` and bypasses the very thing you're testing
Debug toolkit: `curl -svo /dev/null -H 'If-None-Match: "x"' URL`, DevTools Network size column ('disk cache'/'304'), and Chrome's net-export log

Cheat sheet — HTML: `no-cache`; hashed asset: `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`; API GET: `private, no-cache` + ETag; secrets: `no-store`; CDN-heavy page: `max-age=0, s-maxage=600, stale-while-revalidate=60, stale-if-error=86400`
Closing rule: name the cache key, name the TTL, name the invalidation path. If you can't state all three, you don't have a caching strategy
